results.result: The study demonstrates widespread movie-selectivity across the visuo-hippocampal network. Visual areas (LGN, V1, AM-PM) showed the highest prevalence of movie-tuned neurons (89-97%), while hippocampal regions showed substantial but lower prevalence (17-45%), with subiculum having the highest (44.6%) and CA3 the lowest (17.3%) among hippocampal areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C23-C32 provide consistent quantitative data with specific percentages and cell counts across all brain regions. The statistical significance is established (z-scored sparsity >2, p<0.03), and multiple control analyses (stationary epochs, SWR removal, pupil dilation, theta power) confirm the robustness of these findings (C35, C38, C40, C41). The data are internally consistent and supported by appropriate statistical methods.

results.result: Movie tuning persists independently of locomotion and brain state changes. Unlike place cells which require active locomotion and show reduced selectivity during immobility, movie tuning remained intact in both immobile and running mice, and was unaffected by variations in theta power, pupil dilation, or the presence of sharp-wave ripples.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C35, C39-C41 demonstrate movie tuning persistence across behavioral states with appropriate controls. The comparison to place cells (C36) provides important context. Multiple independent control analyses (stationary epochs, theta power, pupil dilation, SWR removal) all support the same conclusion. The statistical rigor is appropriate with proper subsample comparisons to account for data loss.

results.result: Hippocampal neurons have significantly fewer movie-fields per cell (~2) compared to visual neurons (>5), with V1 showing the highest number (10.4±0.1). This is fewer than the number of place-fields reported in comparably long spatial tracks.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C44-C46 provide consistent quantitative data with specific means and SEMs. The comparison to place cells (C46) is appropriately cited. All pairwise comparisons between brain regions were statistically significant (p<0.04 for hippocampal regions, p<7.0×10⁻¹¹ for visual regions), supporting the robustness of these differences.

results.result: Movie-field durations span an unprecedented 1000-fold 'mega-scale' range (0.02s to 20s) across all brain regions, with individual neurons showing 100-fold variation. This is nearly two orders of magnitude greater than previously reported for place cells. Subiculum had the longest fields (3170ms) and V1 the shortest (157ms), though exceptions exist (e.g., LGN fields were twice as long as V1).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C47-C56 provide extensive quantitative characterization of the mega-scale phenomenon with specific measurements and statistical comparisons. The comparison to prior place cell studies (C54, C55) is appropriately cited. The finding is supported across multiple levels: population (C53), individual neurons (C55), and specific brain regions (C47-C52). Control analyses rule out unit isolation artifacts (C105, C106).

results.result: Despite large variations in individual movie-field durations, the total cumulative duration of all movie-fields per cell is remarkably conserved across neurons and brain regions, ranging only from 6.2s (V1) to 10.2s (CA3), spanning about one-fourth of the movie duration.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C57-C59 demonstrate an important organizing principle with specific quantitative data. The 1.66-fold range in cumulative duration contrasts sharply with the >10-fold variation in individual field durations, indicating a compensatory mechanism. Statistical comparisons show visual-hippocampal and visual-visual pairs differ significantly (p<0.001) but hippocampal pairs do not (p>0.07), supporting regional consistency.

results.result: Hippocampal neurons show greater continuous-sequence encoding than visual areas, as evidenced by fewer, broader movie-fields and an eight-fold greater preference for continuous versus scrambled movie sequences. Scrambling virtually abolished hippocampal selectivity (4.4% tuned vs. 17.8% for continuous) but had minimal effect on visual areas (80.4% vs. 92.4%).
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C70-C77, C81-C82, C88 provide converging evidence for sequence-dependent hippocampal encoding. The scrambled movie experiment is well-controlled (same frames, fixed sequence, repeated presentation) and shows statistically significant differences (p<7.4×10⁻⁴ for all regions, p<10⁻¹⁰⁰ for hippocampal vs. visual comparison). The visual continuity index quantifies this difference appropriately. The few hippocampal cells responding to scrambled sequences showed only brief (~50ms) responses (C77), further supporting the sequence-dependence interpretation.

results.result: A subset of neurons across all brain regions, including hippocampus, showed temporally precise movie-fields with elevated spiking restricted to less than 50ms, suggesting temporal coding in addition to rate coding.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 describe a distinct population of neurons with brief responses. The comparison to prior studies in anesthetized cats (C60) is appropriately cited. The finding that such temporal precision exists even in hippocampus (>5 synapses from retina) is notable and well-documented in Figure 2h.

results.result: Population-level analyses reveal that hippocampal regions show broader temporal continuity than visual areas, with weaker correlation between neural and image frame-to-frame changes. Visual cortical areas show stronger modulation in movie segments with greatest frame-to-frame change.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C69 provide population-level characterization consistent with single-neuron findings. The population vector overlap analysis (C63, C64) and frame-to-frame correlation analysis (C65-C68) are appropriate methods. The inverse correlation between frame continuity and ensemble modulation in visual areas (C68) is statistically significant and consistent with prior reports (C69, citing Dyballa et al., 2018).

results.result: Visual cortical neurons responding to scrambled sequences showed more numerous but shorter movie-fields than during continuous presentation. Rearranging scrambled responses by latency could reconstruct continuous movie responses in visual areas but not hippocampus, with latencies following the expected visual hierarchy (LGN: 60ms, V1: 74ms, AM-PM: 91ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 provide important mechanistic insights into how visual versus hippocampal areas process sequences. The rearrangement analysis is methodologically sound and the latency hierarchy (C80, C98) matches anatomical expectations with appropriate citations. The failure of rearrangement in hippocampus (C81, C82) strengthens the sequence-encoding interpretation.

results.result: Population decoding of movie frame number was above chance in all brain regions for continuous movies, most accurate in V1 and least in DG. Scrambled movie decoding was significantly weaker but above chance in visual areas and CA1/subiculum, but not in CA3 and DG.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 demonstrate that neural populations encode movie information decodably. The decoding analysis uses appropriate methods (correlation-based with leave-one-out cross-validation) and controls (shuffled data). The differential performance on scrambled sequences across regions (C85, C86) is consistent with the sequence-encoding hypothesis. Sample size was controlled (150 cells per region) for fair comparison.

results.result: The prevalence of hippocampal movie tuning (32.9%) is comparable to spatial selectivity in rodents and far exceeds that in primates. This dissociation from locomotion-dependent place cell responses agrees with recent reports of dissociated episodic and spatial mechanisms in human amnesia and is consistent with prior human hippocampal movie selectivity studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C95 appropriately contextualize the findings within the broader literature. The comparisons to place cells across species (C90, C91) are well-cited. The connection to human amnesia studies (C92) and prior human single-neuron work (C93, C94) is appropriately qualified. The hypothesis about visual cue representations (C95) is supported by multiple citations across species.

results.result: The mega-scale encoding and hierarchical organization of movie-field properties (duration, tuning strength, sequence preference) can be explained by the anatomical hierarchy of visual processing, with temporal integration windows and intrinsic timescales increasing along the feed-forward pathway from retina to hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C102 provide a coherent theoretical framework supported by appropriate citations. The comparison to prior multi-scale reports (C96) and language processing hierarchies (C97) is well-founded. The latency measurements (C98) directly support the hierarchical interpretation. However, the authors acknowledge exceptions to this pattern (e.g., V1 vs. LGN, CA3 properties), appropriately qualifying the interpretation.

results.result: The longer duration of hippocampal movie-fields could mediate visual chunking or binding of event sequences. Evidence for episodic-like chunking was found in visual areas as well, where scrambled sequences caused fragmentation of movie-fields.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 propose an interpretation about chunking/binding mechanisms. While C104 provides supporting evidence from the scrambled sequence experiment, C103 is explicitly speculative ('could mediate'). The chunking interpretation is plausible given the data but would require additional experiments (e.g., behavioral measures of chunking, manipulation of sequence structure) to be definitively supported.

results.result: Movie-fields are unlikely to arise from the same mechanisms as place-fields based on multiple lines of evidence: (1) mega-scale tuning exists in visual areas where spatial modulation is rare, (2) no neural shutdown during movie presentation unlike spatial exploration, (3) different relationship between firing rate and field number, and (4) poor unit isolation cannot explain mega-scale tuning.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C112 systematically address the alternative hypothesis that movie-fields are place-fields. The arguments are well-reasoned with appropriate citations and control analyses. The unit isolation analysis (C106) directly tests and rules out a technical artifact. The comparison to prior passive viewing studies (C107) appropriately notes key experimental differences. The evidence collectively supports the conclusion that movie-fields represent a distinct phenomenon.

results.result: The findings differ from prior studies of hippocampal responses to moving visual stimuli, which showed single receptive fields lasting a few seconds without mega-scale variation. Hippocampal neurons did not encode simple stimuli (Gabor patches, drifting gratings), indicating the importance of temporally continuous image sequences for hippocampal activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C117 appropriately distinguish the current findings from related prior work. The comparison to the moving bar study (C113, C114) is well-cited and the differences clearly articulated. The lack of response to simple stimuli (C115) is an important control from the same dataset. The connection to sequence coding hypotheses (C116) is appropriately cited, though the proposed role in episodic memory (C117) is explicitly speculative.

results.result: The study analyzed 17,048 broad-spiking putatively excitatory neurons from 24 mice using Neuropixel probes, with mice head-fixed but free to run while viewing a 30-second movie clip monocularly. Statistical significance was determined using z-scored sparsity with threshold >2 (p<0.023).
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22, C121-C127 provide clear methodological details. The use of a publicly available dataset (Allen Brain Observatory) with established spike sorting methods (Kilosort2) enhances reproducibility. The statistical threshold is clearly defined and appropriate. The experimental design is straightforward and well-described.

results.result: Prior work establishes that visual cortical neurons encode movies and show direction selectivity and predictive coding, while hippocampal place cells encode spatial/temporal sequences but typically require locomotion and are thought to be non-sensory. However, the hippocampal encoding of continuous visual sequences (visual episodes) was unknown prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C19 accurately summarize relevant prior literature with appropriate citations. The characterization of the knowledge gap (C19) appropriately motivates the study. The citations appear accurate and relevant to the claims made.

results.result: Movie selectivity was greater than selectivity for classic stimuli (drifting gratings) in V1, consistent with reports of better model fit with natural stimuli for primate visual responses.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 makes a comparison between movie and classic stimuli selectivity, but the authors themselves note that 'direct quantitative comparison across stimuli is difficult' due to differences in presentation parameters (30ms movie frames preceded by similar images vs. 250ms classic stimuli in random order). While the citation to David et al., 2004 supports the general principle, the specific comparison in this dataset may be confounded by methodological differences.

results.result: Movie tuning provides a reliable method to probe visual brain function and bridges the gap between rodent and human hippocampal studies, offering a unified platform to investigate neural mechanisms of episodic coding, learning, and memory across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C89, C118-C120 present appropriate conclusions about the broader implications of the work. The conclusions are well-supported by the data presented and appropriately qualified. The citations to human fMRI studies (C119) and the connection to episodic memory frameworks are reasonable. These represent valid interpretations of the significance of the findings.

results.result: There are other sources of inputs to V1, beyond LGN, that contribute significantly to movie tuning.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 is explicitly presented as 'one possible explanation' for the paradoxical finding that V1 shows stronger movie tuning than LGN. While the citation to Spacek et al., 2022 supports the existence of non-LGN inputs to V1, the claim that these 'contribute significantly to movie tuning' is speculative and not directly tested in this study. Alternative explanations (e.g., cortical processing, recurrent connections) are not ruled out.

results.result: The study reports widespread movie-selectivity across visual and hippocampal regions. Specifically, 97% of thalamo-cortical neurons (LGN, V1, AM-PM) and 33% of hippocampal neurons (DG, CA3, CA1, subiculum) showed significant movie-selectivity, with regional variations (e.g., subiculum 44.6%, CA3 17.3%).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed these findings. One reviewer stated the results 'support a role of rodent hippocampal neurons in general episode encoding' and found the evidence 'convincing.' Another noted the findings were 'substantially more convincing' after revisions addressing behavioral states and ripples. The quantitative prevalence data were not questioned.

results.result: Movie tuning persisted during immobility and across different behavioral states. Movie tuning remained intact when analyzing only stationary epochs, during both high and low theta power periods, and across different pupil dilation states (arousal levels). This contrasts with place cells, which show greatly reduced spatial selectivity during immobility.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised these control analyses. One reviewer stated 'The new analysis on how behavioral states and hippocampal ripples impacted the tuning of movie fields makes the main finding substantially more convincing.' Another noted it was 'particularly helpful that the authors took measures to consider the impact of different states of arousal (pupil diameter), mobility, and SWRs on the expression and significance of movie field tuning.'

results.result: Visual neurons had significantly more movie-fields per cell (>5, with V1 averaging 10.4±0.1) compared to hippocampal neurons (~2, ranging from 2.0±0.02 in CA1 to 2.8±0.3 in CA3). The number of hippocampal movie-fields was smaller than place-fields in comparably long spatial tracks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these quantitative findings. The comprehensive characterization of movie-field properties was noted as a strength, with one reviewer stating 'The properties of movie fields are comprehensively characterized in the manuscript.' The comparison to place cells was accepted without critique.

results.result: Movie-field durations spanned an unprecedented 1000-fold 'mega-scale' range (0.02s to 20s) across all brain regions. The longest fields were in subiculum (3169.9±169.8 ms) and shortest in V1 (156.6±9.2 ms). This mega-scale is nearly two orders of magnitude greater than previous reports in place cells and was observed even within individual neurons showing 100-fold variation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings without challenge. The mega-scale encoding was treated as a novel and important discovery. One reviewer noted the study 'advance[s] understanding of visual information processing across different brain regions,' implicitly accepting the mega-scale characterization as valid and significant.

results.result: Despite tenfold variation in individual movie-field durations between regions, the total cumulative duration of all movie-fields per cell was comparable across neurons and brain regions, ranging from 6.2s (V1) to 10.2s (CA3), spanning about a fourth of the movie duration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question this finding. The comprehensive characterization of movie-field properties, including cumulative durations, was noted as a strength of the analysis. No concerns were raised about this comparative measure across regions.

results.result: Hippocampal responses showed greater continuous-sequence encoding than visual areas, evidenced by fewer and broader movie-fields. Scrambling the movie sequence virtually abolished hippocampal selectivity (90.3% drop in CA1, reducing tuned neurons from 17.8% to 4.4%) but not visual-cortical selectivity. The preference for continuous over scrambled sequences was eight-fold greater in hippocampal than visual areas.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly endorsed this finding. One stated 'The inclusion of neuronal responses to scrambled movie frames in the analysis is a powerful method to reveal the modulation of a key element in episodic events, temporal continuity, on the hippocampal activity.' The scrambled movie experiment was treated as key evidence distinguishing hippocampal episodic encoding from visual feature processing.

results.result: The few hippocampal cells showing selectivity to scrambled sequences had only very short (~50ms) responses, unlike visual cortical neurons which maintained selectivity with more fields of shorter duration. Visual cortical responses to scrambled sequences could be rearranged to resemble continuous movie responses with latencies following visual hierarchy (LGN 60ms, V1 74ms, AM-PM 91ms), but hippocampal responses could not.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as supporting the distinction between visual feature encoding and hippocampal sequence encoding. The latency analysis was not challenged and was treated as consistent with known visual hierarchy. One reviewer appreciated that 'the authors added discussion acknowledging that the cortical processing did not quite follow an apparent hierarchical order,' suggesting acceptance of the overall pattern with noted exceptions.

results.result: Continuous movie decoding was better than chance in all brain regions, most accurate in V1 and least in DG. Scrambled movie decoding was significantly weaker yet above chance in visual areas but not in CA3 and DG. CA1 and subiculum could decode scrambled movie frames slightly above chance levels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the decoding analyses. These results were treated as consistent with and supporting the main findings about differential encoding of continuous versus scrambled sequences across the visual-hippocampal hierarchy.

results.result: Population-level analyses showed that response stability was greater for tuned than untuned neurons, population vector overlap was broader in hippocampal regions indicating longer temporal continuity, and neural frame-to-frame correlations were weaker in hippocampal output regions (CA1, SUB) than visual regions. Movie-code was stronger in segments with greatest frame-to-frame change.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about these population-level analyses. These findings were treated as supporting evidence for the main conclusions about differential encoding properties across the visual-hippocampal hierarchy.

results.result: Control analyses ruled out technical artifacts: neurons recorded simultaneously from the same region showed different selectivity patterns, and there was no significant correlation between unit isolation quality and mega-scale index, arguing against poor spike sorting as an explanation for the findings.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accepted these controls by not raising concerns about data quality or spike sorting. One reviewer noted that 'additional metrics applied (information rate and depth of movie field modulation) substantiate the results,' indicating satisfaction with methodological rigor.

results.result: Movie selectivity was greater than selectivity for classic stimuli like drifting gratings in V1. Hippocampal neurons did not encode Gabor patches or drifting gratings in the same dataset, indicating the importance of temporally continuous sequences for hippocampal activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these comparisons without challenge. The finding that hippocampal neurons require continuous sequences rather than simple stimuli was treated as consistent with the main hypothesis about episodic sequence encoding.

results.result: The average duration of movie-fields increased along the feed-forward hierarchy, consistent with hierarchical organization. Response latency to movie frames followed visual hierarchy (LGN 60ms, V1 74ms, AM-PM 91ms). This hierarchical anatomical organization could explain longer movie-fields, tuning strength, and decoding accuracy in hippocampal regions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted exceptions to the hierarchical pattern. One stated 'It is also appreciated that the authors added discussion acknowledging that the cortical processing did not quite follow an apparent hierarchical order.' This suggests the hierarchical interpretation is partially supported but with acknowledged deviations (e.g., LGN fields being longer than V1).

results.result: The longer duration of hippocampal movie-fields could mediate visual-chunking or binding of event sequences. Evidence for episodic-like chunking was found in visual areas as well, where scrambled sequences caused fragmentation of movie-fields. This is consistent with the hypothesis that hippocampus is involved in coding spatial sequences and episodic memory.
results.evaluation: Reviewers expressed caution about episodic memory claims. One noted 'The Discussion also contains elements that help balance both it and the paper as a whole. It draws a clearer distinction between the representation of visual scenes rather than encoding the contents of episodic memory, clarifying that hippocampal neurons were more likely doing the former than the latter.' This indicates the episodic memory interpretation is speculative rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Movie-fields are unlikely to arise from the same mechanism as place-fields for several reasons: mega-scale fields were found in visual areas far exceeding spatial modulation during virtual navigation; there was no neural shutdown during movie presentation unlike during spatial exploration; and the number of movie-fields was not correlated with firing rate unlike place-fields.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this interpretation. The distinction between movie-fields and place-fields was implicitly accepted through the reviewers' positive assessment of the study's contribution to understanding hippocampal visual encoding, which they treated as distinct from spatial navigation.

results.result: The findings establish movie-coding as a reliable method to probe visual brain function and cognition, opening possibilities for studying thalamic, cortical, and hippocampal regions in a simple passive visual paradigm. The results bridge the gap between rodent and human hippocampal studies and provide a unified platform to investigate episodic coding, learning, and memory.
results.evaluation: Reviewers endorsed these broader implications. One stated the paper 'should be of interest to those studying visual processing as well as those studying visual and spatial coding in the hippocampal system.' Another noted the study 'bridge[s] the long-standing gap between the hippocampal rodent and human studies,' directly affirming this claim.

results.result: The findings are consistent with prior studies showing dissociated mechanisms of episodic encoding and spatial navigation in human amnesia, movie selectivity in human hippocampal neurons, and hippocampal activation in response to movie clip boundaries. The results support the hypothesis that visual cues can create reliable representations across hippocampus in rodents, primates, and humans.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these connections to prior literature without challenge. The consistency with human studies was treated as strengthening the significance of the findings, with one reviewer noting the study 'bridge[s] the long-standing gap between the hippocampal rodent and human studies.'
